newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin's ex-bodyguard seeks political comeback.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin's ex-bodyguard seeks political comeback.

text.p: After a dramatic fall from grace, President Boris Yeltsin's former bodyguard is planning a comeback in a parliamentary by-election in the central Russian town of Tula on Sunday.

Alexander Korzhakov, once a close friend of Yeltsin but ousted last June in a purge of political hawks, is only one of several colourful participants in a baffling race that has brought unaccustomed controversy to this usually quiet provincial city.
The wife of a notorious pyramid investment scheme operator and world-famous chess grandmaster Anatoly Karpov are also running -- to the dismay of local candidates, who call the campaign a "farce".
Korzhakov will be known to most inhabitants of the arms-making city only as the stocky man who used to open and close the door of Yeltsin's limousine, lank strands of hair flapping across his pate.
"These people do not live in Tula and only want the mandate," Tula's liberal candidate Eduard Pashenko told journalists recently. "They do not know the local problems and will never solve them."

Pashenko and some newspapers have complained of campaign manoeuvres by Korzhakov and Yelena Mavrodi, the 27-year-old wife of Sergei Mavrodi, in whose pyramid investment schemes millions of Russians lost their savings two and a half years ago.

Korzhakov, a two-star general viewed suspiciously by liberals and nationalists alike in his days of power as the grey eminence of the Kremlin, was accused of improper campaigning when a local group of war veterans handed out vodka, tea and chocolate to their members -- together with the general's picture.

Korzhakov denies breaking any regulations. "The election commission has not made a single reproach against me," the pugnacious 47-year-old told journalists on his campaign trail in Tula, some 170 km (100 miles) south of Moscow.
He accused his main foe, Kremlin chief of staff Anatoly Chubais, of masterminding a conspiracy to stop his election.
"Chubais and his aides are having long meetings thinking about how to prevent Korzhakov becoming a deputy," he said.

Tula's voters seem split over the right person to represent their town in parliament. "I will certainly vote for someone from Tula," said Shanna, the deputy director of an ice-producing factory, making clear Korzhakov would not get her vote.
An elderly shop-assistant in Tula's Lenin Avenue agreed.
"Korzhakov, Korzhakov, no one here knows Korzhakov."
But the burly ex-KGB general is far from being an outsider.
Some opinion polls suggest he may well gain the seat vacated by another Kremlin foe, Yeltsin's former security adviser Alexander Lebed.

The outspoken Lebed, sacked for insubordination in October, had appeared to form an alliance with Korzhakov and last year endorsed his candidature in the by-election. Now, Lebed has little but scorn for the man he dismisses as just a bodyguard.
Mavrodi, a former model who joined her husband in his get-rich-quick schemes, has dimmer prospects. But there are still queues outside her Tula office.
She launched a cash-for-help bid, handing out 3,000 roubles ($0.55) to everybody who agreed to campaign informally for her. If she succeeds, there are promises of more cash.
The contract specifically allows them to vote for whomever they want. Therefore the cash offer, they calculate, is within the election law.
